## Teaching Philosophy

I view the university classroom as a laboratory for both academic rigor and social engagement — a space to develop skills like public speaking and innovative design alongside moments of enlightenment and deep connection. My teaching is guided by the conviction that these environments can bring political science and peace studies to life in and outside the university, broadening students' sense of purpose while equipping them with hard skills like data literacy and public communication.

In introductory courses, I bridge academic theory and real-world situations through active-learning simulations. For example, in an introductory peace and conflict studies course, I use a "news interview" module in which students provide expert insight into substantive course themes — such as justifications for military intervention or the limits of UN mandates — as guests on a fictional news program. Replaying and critiquing these interviews helps students navigate thorny ethical questions with diplomatic nuance and clarity, turning abstract concepts into tangible communication skills.

In advanced seminars, I prioritize methodology and the knowledge-building process. In data visualization seminars, for example, I task students with replicating the findings and graphics of a peer-reviewed journal article of their choice — forcing them to grapple with real data and its imperfections, and to develop a critical eye for methodology and creativity in presenting results.

This dual focus — outward-facing skills for the real world, and inward-facing mastery of technical knowledge production — is designed to appeal to diverse learning styles, from the aspiring public intellectual to the future quantitative researcher. Whether leading an 80-person lecture or a 15-person seminar, my goal is the same: to turn students from passive consumers of information into active contributors to their fields and to society.
